definition: Fastidious means extremely exacting and hard to please about details.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fastidious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fastidious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Our fastidious neighbor hoses down her recycling before sorting it by color, then by lid.
A particular eater has likes and states them; a fastidious one sends the plate back over the parsley.
Obsessive goes past fastidious — the checking never ends, long after every box has been ticked.

Picky is fastidious in street clothes — the everyday word for the same impossible-to-please fussiness, aimed mostly at choices: toppings sent back, seats swapped, brands refused. Fastidious dresses the trait for formal use and points it at standards and details rather than menus.

Exacting describes the demand itself: a standard set high and enforced, usually on other people's work — the exacting editor requires every rule kept. Fastidious describes the temperament behind such demands, hard to please past reason; meet the exacting bar and you are done, while the fastidious eye keeps hunting.
content with however things turn out
careless of neatness and detail altogether

Latin fastidium built nothing else in English — fastidious is the root's only descendant. One possible ingredient, taedium ("weariness"), did survive on its own as tedium, but that family link is a linguists' guess, not a certainty.
Fastidious means extremely exacting and hard to please about details.
The theater hired the fastidious Marisa Duval to dress one show and kept her for twenty years, though every costume fitting became a small trial.
She sent back three bolts of velvet because the nap ran the wrong way.
Hems were steamed, then checked against a card she carried.
An actress once changed a button backstage; Duval spotted it from the wings at forty feet.
Fastidious is the exact word for Duval because she is extremely exacting and hard to please about details — the bar is the point, and almost nothing clears it.
A meticulous person pours care into their own work; a fastidious one also sits in judgment, finding the flaw in yours.
The word carries that faint chill of a bar set impossibly high.
Fastidious describes the person almost nothing satisfies — taste sharpened into squeamishness.
Keep the family straight: this unit's meticulous praises care spent on one's own work; methodical describes ordered steps; scrupulous adds a moral conscience.
Fastidious alone implies that pleasing its owner is nearly impossible — use it when the bar, not the effort, is the story.

The model shipwrights' club has one member nobody wants to follow at the workbench.
Anders is fastidious in a way the others find almost painful to watch.
He ties each rigging knot with tweezers, compares it to a photograph under a loupe, and cuts it away if the loop sits a hair too wide.
The club's judges have told him twice that no scoring category exists for the underside of a hull.
He planks the undersides anyway, because he would know they were bare, even if no judge ever turned the ship over.
